title: The Hill at Dusk

setup.context: When I was twenty-five, I climbed the hill above our town at the end of a bad week. I had climbed it many times before. That evening was different.

paragraphs.text: I was twenty-five. I had the export business my uncle had given me, a motorcycle I loved too much, and a reputation for getting things done. From outside it looked like a good life.
I had lost a large order that month. Nothing dramatic. A shipment held at a port for three weeks, a buyer who stopped answering. I was furious, mostly at myself.
That evening I climbed the old steps up Ratan Hill. There is a small temple at the top with a bell nobody rings anymore. I sat on the step below it and watched the lights come on in the town.

I did not have a revelation. I had a plain thought: that I was spending my life running from one problem to the next and calling it being successful. It wasn't a cruel thought. It just wasn't comfortable.
I walked down in the dark. I did not sleep much that night, and the next morning I started to change how I ran the business. Slowly, which was the only way I could do it.

reflection.insight: A bad week can be the first honest hour you have had in a long time. Most of us need a place to sit where nothing is asking anything of us.
reflection.question: Where do you go when you need to stop being useful for an hour?

follow_up_options: What did the temple look like?

responses_to_follow_ups.changed: Not dramatically. I hired a better manager and stopped answering every phone call. The business grew more slowly after that, but I was less tired, and my uncle said I had finally started to look like I knew what I was doing.
responses_to_follow_ups.temple: Small. Whitewashed, with a crack in the bell. The priest was an old man who sold marigolds at the foot of the steps. He never asked me what was wrong, which is why I kept going back.
responses_to_follow_ups.climb: Less often than I should. When I do, I sit on the same step. The town looks smaller from there, and that helps.
